newsitem.title: GERMANY: German conservatives blast FDP for tax-cut calls.
newsitem.headline: German conservatives blast FDP for tax-cut calls.

text.p: Conservative German political leaders accused their Free Democrat partners in government on Tuesday of pursuing narrow self-interest in demanding tax cuts, saying the move could jeopardise the ruling coalition.

Leaders of the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party to Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), warmed up to the start of a three-day party conference on Wednesday with a series of broadsides against the liberal FDP.
"A coalition will not work if one party is constantly trying to raise its own profile at the expense of its partners," said CSU general secretary Bernd Protzner in an interview with German Radio.

"But that is exactly what the FDP is doing. The Free Democrats have to stop this one-dimensional catering to their special interest groups. Otherwise, it is possible that the coalition will be endangered."

The FDP angered the Bavarian conservatives on Monday at their own party conference in Stuttgart, where they demanded the abolition by 2000 of a widely loathed "solidarity tax" levied to rebuild eastern Germany.
The renewed calls to eliminate the tax by the FDP came just weeks after the coalition reached a fragile truce over the same issue.

Kohl's 14-year-old coalition nearly collapsed in late 1996 when the FDP pressed for a two-point cut in the tax to 5.5 percent in 1998. Despite fierce opposition from the CDU/CSU, the cut was agreed just before Christmas.
But the peace and harmony did not last long.

With opinion polls showing the FDP rebounding slightly from its once precarious position near the five percent hurdle required to remain in parliament, the party's focus on tax cuts has touched a nerve with voters -- and its coalition partners.

"What bothers us is that the FDP is constantly harking on the subject of taxes in a way that makes it seem as if Finance Minister (Theo) Waigel needs extra help with his homework," said Michael Glos, CSU parliamentary party leader in Bonn.
Glos told SWF1 radio that the FDP had no business sticking its nose into the business of Waigel, who is also the leader of the CSU.
"They can't live off an issue that in principle is none of their business," Glos said. "That was really very, very hard for us to accept."
Erwin Huber, finance minister in Bavaria, said the FDP was just "throwing sand" in the eyes of the voters with their tax-cutting appeals.

"The FDP suggestions to eliminate the solidarity tax are not financially sound, have little credibility and are thus pure propaganda," Huber told ARD television. "Anyone who wilfully throws sand in the eyes of the voters like that is being cocky and guilty of negligence."
Kohl's CDU has already repudiated the FDP demand in the bluntest terms, saying anyone seeking the surcharge's abolition had no right to be taken seriously.

The renewed tax row comes just as a coalition working group is finalising tax reforms aimed at making big cuts in income tax while ensuring Germany can still stick to the borrowing limits required under projected European monetary union.
